referee: The AI matches your key: standard array merge sort needs an O(n) temporary merge buffer plus O(log n) recursion-stack space, for O(n) auxiliary space overall.
ai: O(n) extra memory. The merge step can't safely be done in place: as you pick the smallest element from the left or right half, you need somewhere to put it without overwriting elements not yet merged. So you copy into a temporary buffer of up to n elements (the lecture's 'second shelf'), then copy back. A single buffer of size n can be allocated once and reused across all merges, because merges at the same recursion level use disjoint pieces and merges at different levels happen at different times. If you instead allocate new arrays at each call, the total is still O(n) live at any time, since sizes shrink as n + n/2 + n/4 + ... ≈ 2n. The recursion stack adds O(log n), which is dominated by O(n). So total auxiliary space is O(n), the lecture's 'twice as much space' trade-off for speed.

ai: The base case is n == 1 (or n <= 1, which also covers 0 and guards against negative input), and it returns 1. Since factorial(n) = n * factorial(n-1), each recursive call hands itself a smaller problem, and the chain must stop at a case whose answer is known immediately. Example: int factorial(int n) { if (n <= 1) return 1; return n * factorial(n - 1); }.
